name: Technology Adoption Curves
subject: quantum-computing
subjectTitle: A Skeptic's Guide to Quantum Computing

lesson.title: Being Ready Is Not the Same as Being Wanted
lesson.summary: Even a technology that reaches full maturity on the TRL scale still has to travel through a separate, well studied adoption curve of skeptical buyer segments before it becomes a mainstream commercial success.
lesson.body:
Everett Rogers' diffusion of innovations research, first published in 1962 and refined across decades of subsequent study, describes how new technologies spread through a market over time by dividing adopters into segments based on how quickly they are willing to try something new. Innovators, typically a very small slice of any market, adopt first, often for the sake of novelty itself and a high tolerance for rough edges. Early adopters follow, willing to accept real risk and an imperfect product in exchange for a genuine strategic or competitive advantage. The early and late majority, together the bulk of any market, adopt only once a technology is proven, standardized, and de-risked by the experience of those who came before them. Laggards adopt last, sometimes only when the older alternative is no longer available at all.

This is a necessary complement to Technology Readiness Levels because the two scales measure different things. TRL measures whether a technology itself works reliably. The adoption curve measures whether, once it works, the market is willing to buy and depend on it. A technology can reach TRL 9, fully proven, and still spend years moving through the adoption curve, because buyers past the earliest segment need reliability evidence, trained talent, supporting tools, and a track record from similar organizations before committing.

Electric vehicles illustrate this well. The core technology, batteries and motors, had cleared very high TRL levels, essentially proven, well before mainstream buyers purchased in large numbers. The gap between it works and the mainstream buys it was measured in years of adoption curve progress: innovators and early adopters bought for years while most buyers waited for lower prices, more charging infrastructure, and proof from peers that the cars were reliable. Quantum computing, even if its hardware eventually reaches TRL 9, should face a similar separate adoption lag, not an instant rush of mainstream customers the moment a lab demonstration succeeds.

For revenue and valuation, tracked under Market Valuation vs Revenue, this means even a technically successful quantum computer will likely see revenue climb slowly through a small early adopter base for a meaningful stretch before, if ever, reaching the much larger early majority market. Investors pricing these stocks today are making two stacked bets: that the hardware climbs the entire readiness ladder, and that once it does, the market adopts it briskly rather than slowly. Both have to pay off for today's valuations to make sense, and the second is largely independent of how the physics turns out.

Between early adopters and the much larger early majority sits a specific, well documented danger zone where many promising technologies stall out permanently. That gap has its own name, taken up next.
